clinicalPearls: A distinctive nystagmus in which one eye rises and intorts while the other falls and extorts, then the cycle reverses, resembling a see-saw
The pendular form is classically associated with parasellar or suprasellar masses compressing the chiasm and optic pathways
A bitemporal hemianopia frequently accompanies the pendular form because of chiasmal involvement
The jerk (hemi-see-saw) form points to a mesodiencephalic lesion, often in the region of the interstitial nucleus of Cajal
It may also occur with severe congenital visual loss and some retinal dystrophies
MRI directed at the sellar, suprasellar and mesodiencephalic regions is central to the workup
reference.pathophysiology: See-saw nystagmus arises from disruption of the vestibulo-ocular and visual pathways that coordinate torsional and vertical eye movements, particularly around the diencephalon and rostral midbrain. The pendular form is linked to large parasellar or suprasellar lesions that damage the chiasm and adjacent structures, plausibly removing visual and vestibular stabilising signals, whereas the jerk hemi-see-saw form reflects a focal lesion of the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and its connections. The result is the conjugate torsional and disjunctive vertical oscillation that defines the sign.
additionalDifferentials: Other acquired pendular nystagmus (for example demyelinating)
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain focused on the sellar, suprasellar and mesodiencephalic regions
Formal visual field testing for a bitemporal hemianopia
Endocrine evaluation if a sellar mass is found
Electroretinography when a retinal cause is suspected
redFlags: Bitemporal hemianopia or other chiasmal field loss
Signs of a sellar or suprasellar mass, including endocrine disturbance
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; the nystagmus may improve if a compressive lesion is treated, but it can persist, and associated visual field loss may not fully recover.
pitfalls: Failing to image the sella and chiasm when see-saw nystagmus is identified
Not distinguishing the pendular from the jerk (hemi-see-saw) form and their different localisations
Missing a congenital or retinal cause in a child
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
